title: Confusion and a sodium of 118
presentation: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter for two days of worsening confusion and one episode of vomiting. She has no headache, fever, or focal weakness. Triage labs: Na 118 mEq/L, K 4.0, glucose 104, creatinine 0.7.

stages.label: History
stages.text: Past history: hypertension, COPD. Medications: amlodipine, tiotropium, and an albuterol inhaler. No diuretics, no SSRIs, no recent medication changes. She has smoked a pack a day for 40 years. Her daughter mentions she has lost about 5 kg over three months and has had a dry cough for six weeks. No vomiting or diarrhoea before the last two days. She drinks two cups of coffee a day and no excess water.
stages.prompt: What is your initial differential for her hyponatremia, and what do you want to know next?
stages.learner_goal: Build a broad differential for hyponatremia organised by volume status, and ask for volume assessment before committing.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: BP 138/82, HR 84, afebrile, SpO2 94% on air. Moist mucous membranes, no orthostatic drop, JVP normal, no peripheral oedema, no ascites. Chest: scattered wheeze, reduced breath sounds at the right upper zone. Neuro: oriented to person only, no focal deficits, no asterixis.
stages.prompt: Does the exam change your differential? Commit to your top two causes and tell me which test separates them.
stages.learner_goal: Recognise euvolemia and move to urine studies.

stages.label: Labs
stages.text: Serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality 452 mOsm/kg. Urine sodium 64 mEq/L. TSH 1.9 mIU/L. 8 AM cortisol 18 mcg/dL. Uric acid 2.6 mg/dL. Chest radiograph: 3 cm right hilar mass with right upper lobe volume loss.
stages.prompt: Put it together. What is the unifying diagnosis, and what is the first thing you do for her sodium tonight?
stages.learner_goal: Name SIADH with a likely malignant cause and choose management proportional to symptom severity.

diagnosis: SIADH secondary to small cell lung cancer
key_clues: Euvolemic on exam (no orthostasis, normal JVP, no oedema)
Urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg despite serum hypo-osmolality
Urine sodium > 30 mEq/L with no diuretic
40 pack-year smoker with weight loss, cough, and a hilar mass
Low uric acid supports SIADH over hypovolemia

distractors.name: Hypovolemic hyponatremia from vomiting
distractors.why_not: Vomiting began after the confusion; exam is euvolemic and urine sodium is high.

distractors.name: Thiazide-induced hyponatremia
distractors.why_not: No thiazide on the medication list.

distractors.name: Adrenal insufficiency
distractors.why_not: Morning cortisol is 18; no hyperkalaemia or hypotension.

distractors.name: Primary polydipsia or beer potomania
distractors.why_not: Urine osmolality is high; polydipsia gives maximally dilute urine.

distractors.name: Pseudohyponatremia
distractors.why_not: Measured serum osmolality is genuinely low.

rubric.description: Asks about or assesses volume status before committing to a cause
rubric.concept: Hyponatremia is classified by volume status before anything else

rubric.description: Differential includes SIADH, a hypovolemic cause, and an endocrine cause (thyroid or adrenal)
rubric.concept: The euvolemic hyponatremia differential: SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, polydipsia, low solute intake

rubric.description: Orders urine osmolality and urine sodium as the discriminating tests
rubric.concept: Urine osmolality and urine sodium are the first branch points in hyponatremia

rubric.description: Checks serum osmolality to exclude pseudohyponatremia or hyperglycaemia
rubric.concept: Confirm true hypotonic hyponatremia before working it up

rubric.description: Requests TSH and cortisol before labelling SIADH
rubric.concept: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion; thyroid and adrenal function must be normal

rubric.description: Connects the smoking history, weight loss, cough, or hilar mass to a paraneoplastic cause
rubric.concept: New SIADH in a smoker is small cell lung cancer until proven otherwise

rubric.description: Management is proportional to symptoms: hypertonic saline bolus for moderate to severe symptoms, otherwise fluid restriction
rubric.concept: Symptomatic hyponatremia: 100-150 mL 3% saline bolus, target rise 4-6 mEq/L in the first 6 hours

rubric.description: Mentions a correction ceiling (about 8 mEq/L per 24 h) or the risk of osmotic demyelination
rubric.concept: Limit sodium correction to about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination

management_summary: She is moderately symptomatic (confusion), so give a 100-150 mL bolus of 3% saline, recheck sodium in 20 minutes and repeat up to twice, aiming for a 4-6 mEq/L rise in the first 6 hours and no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. Then fluid restrict and treat the cause. Urgent CT chest and tissue diagnosis for the hilar mass.
teaching_points: Classify hyponatremia by tonicity first, then volume status, then urine osmolality and sodium. The exam is the first test.
Urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg with serum hypo-osmolality means ADH is acting; in a euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function that is SIADH.
SIADH has a cause. In a smoker with weight loss, image the chest the same day.
Symptoms, not the number, decide treatment urgency. Moderate or severe symptoms get hypertonic saline; the correction ceiling is about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21e, Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances
Verbalis JG et al. Diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of hyponatremia: expert panel recommendations. Am J Med 2013;126(10 Suppl 1):S1-42
Spasovski G et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia. Eur J Endocrinol 2014
